strengths: The paper focuses on an important capability of ML models, the capacity to express uncertainty when appropriate.
They introduce a large and diverse dataset to explicitly assess uncertainty of VLMs in a VQA setting.
Different sources of uncertainty are nicely categorized into a taxonomy, and questions are collected according to this taxonomy.
Moreover the same image contains both answerable and unanswerable questions in their dataset, providing a nice contrastive setup.

They benchmark SoTA VLMs against their dataset, and show that fine-tuning these models on their dataset leads to better performance on both their dataset and on other relevant datasets (refusal-based, hallucinations).
Experiments seem reasonably thorough across different datasets and metrics are broken down for different types of uncertainty.
The work aims to address the important problem of uncertainty in VLMs. An interesting and valuable benchmark is proposed.
The work shows clear experimental evidence that demonstrates the improvements from fine-tuning with the proposed dataset.
The experimental results provide clear evidence of the benefits of the proposed dataset. The fine-tuned model with CERTAINLYUNCERTAIN shows performance gains and improved calibration.
The paper is well-written with clear presentation.

Well-Designed Benchmark Dataset: The authors carefully provide a rigorous classification of uncertainties into two high-level types (epistemic and aleatoric) with six finer categories. The development of 178K samples through a synthetic data pipeline and human curation reflects commendable effort.

Innovative Metric: The proposed confidence-weighted accuracy offers a comprehensive evaluation by factoring both the correctness and confidence of predictions, penalizing overconfident errors while rewarding high-confidence correct answers.

Comprehensive Experiments: The paper explores multiple training paradigms, including fine-tuning, R-tuning, and preference optimization, across a range of benchmarks. Results highlight both the importance of addressing uncertainty and the effectiveness of the proposed dataset.
weaknesses: Dataset quality is a concern; unclear whether a similar filtration process was applied to the training set for the extraneous questions or to questions generated from image captions, and request clarification on the 93% number quoted in Ln 239.

The lack of qualitative examples makes the results difficult to read; some qualitative analysis in the results would be helpful, e.g., showing how training on the dataset causes the model to perform better on uncertainty questions compared to the base model.
Clarity of the paper could be improved significantly; certain terminology such as the LAVE method is introduced without proper explanation.
More explanation on the hallucination-based benchmarks would be helpful.
The experiments section is quite dense with large tables; it is unclear whether the entirety of Table 4 needs to be presented or whether some numbers can be moved to the Appendix.

The paper would benefit from a background section that explains key concepts such as VLMs and SoTA models, common metrics for evaluating uncertainty capabilities, and fine-tuning strategies; related work is dense and would also benefit from clearer explanations.

It is not clear whether the questions are from the original dataset and only the images are perturbed, or whether the questions are generated from GPT4-V after the image perturbation has been applied (Lns 195-196 vs. 198-200).

The process of deriving contrastive instances ... is unclear how those instances are classified into the predefined uncertainty types (Epistemic, Aleatoric); the criteria for distinguishing between epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty in the generated QA pairs is not well-defined.

The dataset shows bias: a high proportion of QA pairs is categorized as “extraneous awareness”, which could lead to models being over-optimized for this specific type of uncertainty, potentially hindering their ability to generalize to other types.
It would be helpful to know the human performance on this benchmark for comparison; without this baseline, it's hard to gauge how challenging the benchmark is.

Limited Model Coverage: As a benchmark, the number of models evaluated is not sufficient; only GPT-4V was evaluated for closed-source models, and recent advanced open-source models such as InternVL2, Qwen2-VL, and LLaVA-Onevision were not tested.

Limited Evaluation: Most experiments focus on refusal-oriented tasks with fewer hallucination-related benchmarks; expanding evaluations to include hallucination datasets like HalluBench [1] and SHR [2], along with general benchmarks such as MME and MMBench, would provide a better view.

Concern of Data Proportion: As seen in Table 1, the "Extraneous" awareness category has a higher data ratio compared to other categories; a clearer explanation for this design choice would be beneficial.

Concern of "Complexity Awareness" in the benchmark: Certain examples under "complexity awareness" seem to fall into a gray area; for instance, the query regarding the number of balloons forming "30" could reasonably expect an approximate answer rather than an IDK response, and similarly for the "distance between the two cats".
